Workshop 3 · Sessions 7–9 · Thursday 15 October 2026

Guess the next word: language models built by counting

Type "thank" on your phone and the keyboard offers "you". How does it know? It has read a lot of text and counted what usually comes next. Today you build the same thing from a dozen short sentences, in plain Python, fix its biggest weakness, and measure how good it is.

Open slides Notebooks and data Practice problems

By the end of this workshop you can

  • explain what a language model does: it gives every possible next word a probability
  • count bigrams (pairs of neighbouring words) and turn the counts into next-word probabilities, by hand and in Python
  • work out the probability of a short sentence by multiplying its steps
  • explain why a word pair never seen before gets probability 0, and fix it with add-one and add-k smoothing
  • compare two models with perplexity on text they have not seen: lower means less surprised

Course outcome CO1 · Reading: [SLP] Chapter 3

Before class: pre-read

1. Checklist

  • git pull run in your ADS6703 folder, so the three Workshop 3 notebooks are in ADS6703/w03/
  • The Workshop 2 practice problems tried

2. Where you already use a language model

A language model is a program that guesses the next word. More exactly: it gives every possible next word a probability. You use one many times a day:

  • the three suggestions above your phone keyboard
  • the search box that finishes your question as you type
  • voice typing, which has to decide whether you said "recognise speech" or "wreck a nice beach"
  • chatbots, which write their answer one guessed word at a time

The big ones are very complicated. The idea underneath is not, and today we build it with nothing but counting.

3. The whole idea in five minutes

Counting pairs. Here are four tiny sentences. We add <s> at the start of each sentence and </s> at the end, so we can also guess the first word, and know when a sentence is finished:

<s> i like tea </s>
<s> i like coffee </s>
<s> you like tea </s>
<s> i drink tea </s>

A pair of neighbouring words is called a bigram. After i we see like twice and drink once. So, in these sentences, the probability that like comes after i is 2 out of 3:

P(like | i) = count of i like ÷ count of i = 2/3

Read P(like | i) as "the probability of like, given i".

A whole sentence. Multiply the steps, like the chance of two heads in a row is ½ × ½:

Step P(i | <s>) P(like | i) P(tea | like) P(</s> | tea) Sentence
i like tea 3/4 2/3 2/3 3/3 1/3

The zero problem. "you drink tea" is a perfectly good sentence, but you drink never appears, so P(drink | you) = 0 and the whole sentence gets 0. Smoothing fixes this by pretending every pair was seen a little more often than it really was.

Perplexity scores a model on text it has never seen: on average, how many words was it choosing between? A model that gives each real next word a probability of ¼ is as unsure as someone picking one of 4 words: perplexity 4. Lower is better.

4. Read

  • [SLP] Jurafsky & Martin, Chapter 3, N-gram Language Models: the sections on n-grams, on evaluating language models (training and test sets, perplexity), on sampling sentences, and on smoothing (Laplace and add-k). Skip the maths of log probabilities and entropy: we don't need it.

5. Practise: counting words and pairs in Python

Open ADS6703/w03/W03-0-counting-pairs.ipynb. It uses the four tiny sentences above and covers exactly the Python the in-class notebooks need: Counter, pairs of neighbours with zip, a loop that finds what comes after a word, turning counts into fractions, and picking a word at random by its count. Plain Python only: no pandas, no data files. Five short self-checking exercises.

6. Try (optional)

On your phone, type each of these and write down the three suggested next words:

thank        happy        I would like a cup of        see you

Then tap the middle suggestion ten times in a row and read the sentence it makes. Bring it to class.

Handout: language model cheat sheet

Print this page, or keep it open during the labs.

Words

language model gives every possible next word a probability
unigram one word on its own, no context
bigram a pair of neighbouring words
trigram three neighbouring words
<s>, </s> made-up words for the start and end of a sentence
training text what the model counts
test text held back, to score the model fairly

Formulas

P(next | word) count(word next) ÷ count(word)
sentence multiply every step
add-one (count(word next) + 1) ÷ (count(word) + V)
add-k (count(word next) + k) ÷ (count(word) + k·V)
V how many different next words there are

Perplexity

meaning on average, how many words the model is choosing between
every word ½ perplexity 2
every word ¼ perplexity 4
½ then ⅛ ½ × ⅛ = 1/16 → 16 → √16 = 4
lower better
in Python (1 / product) ** (1 / N)

Worked example: four tiny sentences

<s> i like tea </s> · <s> i like coffee </s> · <s> you like tea </s> · <s> i drink tea </s>

After… comes… count probability add-one (V = 7)
<s> i 3 3/4 4/11
<s> you 1 1/4 2/11
i like 2 2/3 3/10
i drink 1 1/3 2/10
you like 1 1/1 2/8
you drink 0 0 1/8

V = 7 possible next words: i, you, like, drink, tea, coffee, </s>.

Python

["<s>"] + words + ["</s>"] mark the start and end
zip(words, words[1:]) every word with the next one
Counter() · .update(pairs) count the pairs
for (w1, w2), n in pair_counts.items(): go through every pair and its count
random.choices(words, weights=counts)[0] pick a word in proportion to its count
(1 / product) ** (1 / N) perplexity from the product of N probabilities
